commands.description: Evaluates the expression in the file `PATH` names, or its `default.nix` when `PATH` is a directory, the file the search path finds for `<NAME>`, or the expression `--expr` gives, and prints its value as `nix-instantiate --eval` prints it. With an argument from `--arg` or `--argstr`, the value is called first, as `nix-instantiate --eval` calls it: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. Without one it is not called, and a function prints as `<LAMBDA>`; with `--aterm` it is called either way, as `nix-instantiate` calls it before it writes a derivation. A part of the value the evaluation never needed prints as `<CODE>`; with `--strict` the whole value is evaluated first. A relative path resolves against the file's directory, or for `--expr` and an `--arg` expression against the working directory. A `<name>` path, and a `<NAME>` argument, is looked up in the entries `--nix-path` adds, then `NIX_PATH`'s, then the `<nix/*>` expressions nova-nix ships with. An evaluation that writes to the store, as `builtins.toFile`, `builtins.path` and the fetchers do, stops with an error at its first write to a store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed; one that writes nothing is not refused. With `NOVA_NIX_C_STATS` set to a file, an evaluation that succeeds writes to it a census of the memory its C data layer holds: the objects and bytes of each kind allocated, those its result, the root environment, the import cache and the search path still reach, and what finding them cost. With `NOVA_NIX_REGION_STATS` set to a file, it writes a census of regions: at the end of each force of a thunk, the bytes the force allocated and the bytes of them still reachable, and the most bytes collectors freeing at those points would have held.

commands.description: Evaluates the file `PATH` names, or its `default.nix` when `PATH` is a directory, the file the search path finds for `<NAME>`, or the expression `--expr` gives, selects the attribute `-A` names when it is given, builds the derivation that results and every derivation it depends on, and prints the path of the output its `outputName` names, the first of its outputs unless the expression selects another, as `nix-build` does. Before each component of the `-A` path is selected from it, and once the path has selected it, the value is called as `nix-build` calls it, with the arguments from `--arg` and `--argstr` or with none: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. A derivation whose outputs a substituter holds is downloaded instead of built, from the substituters `nix.conf` configures and the one `--substituter` adds, and only a path signed by a trusted key is accepted. The outputs of a derivation whose `allowSubstitutes` attribute is false are built instead, unless `always-allow-substitutes` is on. A substituter that fails stops the build unless `fallback` is on. With `--check` the derivation is checked as `nix-build --check` checks one: an output of its that is not valid is first downloaded from a substituter that holds it, the derivations it depends on are built or downloaded as ever, and then it is built again beside its outputs, never downloaded, and each output is compared with the one in the store. The rebuild changes nothing in the store and what it wrote is discarded; the downloads and builds before it add to the store as in any build. An output that comes out different fails the command with status 104, so a path a substituter supplied can be held to a build. The output is linked from `./result`, or from the path `--out-link` gives, with `-NAME` appended for an output `NAME` other than `out`, as `nix-build` links it, and the link is a root the garbage collector keeps; it replaces a link already there that points into the store, and anything else there fails the command. With `--no-out-link` nothing is linked. A store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed, is refused before anything is evaluated.

commands.description: Evaluates the file `PATH` names, or its `default.nix` when `PATH` is a directory, the file the search path finds for `<NAME>`, or the expression `--expr` gives, selects the attribute `-A` names when it is given, and reports what the closure of the derivation that results relies on. Before each component of the `-A` path is selected from it, and once the path has selected it, the value is called as `nix-build` calls it, with the arguments from `--arg` and `--argstr` or with none: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. A closure bottoms out in fixed-output derivations, whose outputs are held to the hash their recipe states, whether a builtin fetches them or the closure builds them. First come those a build runs as builders, where a derivation's builder is inside one's output, or inside the tree a builtin such as `builtin:unpack` makes from it and any others; then those whose files hold prebuilt code, each with the files found; then those not fully read, each with what was not. Each says whether a builtin fetched it or the closure built it, and names any other with the same hash. Then come how many hold no prebuilt code, the builders the closure does not contain, such as a program on the host, the builders in its input sources, the builtins nova-nix runs itself, and how many input sources its derivations take, store paths none of them builds. A fixed-output derivation whose builder is a builtin and which has no inputs is fetched first, or downloaded from a substituter, so that its bytes can be read; any other is only downloaded, with the paths it references, from a substituter that holds it, since making it would run its builder, and is read only when one does or the store already holds it. A fetch that fails stops the command, and so does a failed download of one that no builtin fetches. The scan finds prebuilt code by its header: a PE image, an ELF or Mach-O file, a COFF object, or an ar archive, whose members it does not read. It looks in a fetched file, in each file of a fetched tree, and in each file of a tar archive, plain or compressed with gzip, bzip2, xz or zstd, that one of those is; it does not open an archive inside another, and it reports a file in another archive format it knows, such as zip, as not read. It reports what the closure relies on, not whether any of it is safe. A store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed, is refused before anything is fetched or read.

commands.description: Copies the closure of each `PATH`, or with `--all` every valid path except derivations, to the binary cache at `URL`. A `PATH` is a store path, in full or as its base name; a derivation is refused, since a binary cache serves outputs. Paths the cache already holds are skipped, and every NAR is in place before any narinfo announces it. An `http://` or `https://` `URL` is a nova-cache server, which signs what it receives, and a narinfo is read back to check that the server signed it. A `file://` `URL` names a directory, which gets the layout upstream's `nix copy --to file://` writes, so that any web server can serve it: `nix-cache-info`, a narinfo for each path, signed with the secret key in `--secret-key-file`, and the NARs under `nar/`. The key file is one `nix-store --generate-binary-cache-key` writes, and a substituter of the cache trusts its public key. It prints how many paths it pushed and how many the cache already held.

commands.description: Deletes every store path no root keeps, directly or through the paths that reference it, and prints how many it deleted and the space it freed, as `nix-store --gc` does. The roots are the links `build` made to its outputs, while they stay, and the links and files under the store's `.nova-nix/gcroots` directory; a path a running program has open is not a root, and a rooted output does not keep the `.drv` that built it. A store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed, is refused. With `--print-roots` it lists the roots and deletes nothing.

configuration.description: `nix.conf` is read in upstream's order: `$NIX_CONF_DIR/nix.conf`, where `NIX_CONF_DIR` defaults to `/etc/nix`, or `%ProgramData%\nix` on Windows; the XDG `nix/nix.conf` files or `$NIX_USER_CONF_FILES`; then `$NIX_CONFIG`. A later source replaces an earlier one's value, an `extra-` prefix on a list setting adds to it instead, and a flag adds to whatever they configure: an entry to a list, or a Boolean moved from its default, which a flag cannot move back.

global.description: nova-nix evaluates Nix expressions, builds derivations, reports what a derivation's closure relies on, pushes store paths to a binary cache and maintains its store, one command per invocation, and reads its settings from `nix.conf` as upstream Nix does. Each command takes the flags listed with it, after the command's name. A command exits with status 0 when it succeeds, and with status 1 when it fails, after saying why on stderr; `build --check` alone has another status, 104, for an output that differs.
